1.  **Headed chances.** Let's say that you want to estimate the probability that a headed chance at this level of football is scored.
    Marta Vidal has asked for a defensible figure before the club weighs a bid for a target man whose game is built on winning crosses.
    You pull every shot taken with the head at the 2022 Men's World Cup[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-1] and find that 28 of the 252 headed shots were scored.
    Recall from @sec-case-study-med-consult that for a question about the *process* — how headed chances convert at this level, at the next tournament, for Northbridge — these 252 shots are a sample, and the long-run conversion rate of headed chances is unknown.
    You decide to create a bootstrap interval from the original sample of 252 shots.

    ```r
    wc2022_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv")

    headed_shots <- wc2022_shots |> filter(body_part == "Head")

    headed_shots |>
      summarize(shots = n(), goals = sum(goal), conversion = mean(goal))
    #> # A tibble: 1 × 3
    #>   shots goals conversion
    #>   <int> <int>      <dbl>
    #> 1   252    28      0.111

    set.seed(1205)
    headed_boot <- headed_shots |>
      mutate(result = if_else(goal, "goal", "no goal")) |>
      specify(response = result, success = "goal") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
      calculate(stat = "prop")

    round(quantile(headed_boot$stat, c(0.025, 0.05, 0.95, 0.975)), 3)
    #>  2.5%    5%   95% 97.5%
    #> 0.075 0.083 0.143 0.151

    ggplot(headed_boot, aes(x = stat)) +
      geom_histogram(binwidth = 1 / 252) +
      labs(
        x = "Bootstrapped proportion of headed shots scored",
        y = "Count",
        title = "1,000 bootstrapped proportions"
      )
    ```

    The histogram of the 1,000 bootstrapped proportions is roughly bell-shaped and centered at the observed proportion (the mean of the 1,000 values is 0.111), with the bootstrapped proportions stepping in increments of $1/252$ and ranging from about $0.056$ to $0.171.$
    Four of its percentiles are printed above.

    a.  Describe in words the relevant statistic and parameter for this problem.
        If you know the numerical value for either one, provide it.
        If you don't know the numerical value, explain why the value is unknown.

    b.  What notation is used to describe, respectively, the statistic and the parameter?

    c.  If using software to bootstrap the original dataset, what is the statistic calculated on each bootstrap sample?

    d.  When creating a bootstrap sampling distribution (histogram) of the bootstrapped sample proportions, where should the center of the histogram lie?

    e.  The code above printed four percentiles of the 1,000 bootstrapped sample proportions.
        Using the appropriate pair, construct a 90% confidence interval for the probability that a headed chance is scored.

    f.  Interpret the confidence interval in the context of the data.

2.  **Right-footed shots at the Women's Euro.** Scouting reports habitually flag a prospect's weaker foot, so Priya Rao wants a tournament baseline: what proportion of shots at this level arrive on the right foot?
    At the 2025 Women's Euro, 502 of the 913 shots — a proportion of $502/913 = 0.55$ — were taken with the right foot.[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-2]
    However, this value is based on a single tournament's worth of shots, so it may not be a perfect estimate for the population parameter of interest on its own.
    The seeded code below bootstraps the sample 1,000 times.

    ```r
    weuro2025_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/weuro2025_shots.csv")

    weuro2025_shots |>
      mutate(part = if_else(body_part == "Right Foot", "right foot", "other")) |>
      count(part)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 2
    #>   part           n
    #>   <chr>      <int>
    #> 1 other        411
    #> 2 right foot   502

    set.seed(1206)
    rightfoot_boot <- weuro2025_shots |>
      mutate(part = if_else(body_part == "Right Foot", "right foot", "other")) |>
      specify(response = part, success = "right foot") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
      calculate(stat = "prop")

    round(quantile(rightfoot_boot$stat, c(0.01, 0.04, 0.96, 0.99)), 3)
    #>    1%    4%   96%   99%
    #> 0.514 0.521 0.581 0.587

    ggplot(rightfoot_boot, aes(x = stat)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
      labs(
        x = "Bootstrapped proportion of right-footed shots",
        y = "Count",
        title = "1,000 bootstrapped proportions"
      )
    ```

    The histogram of the 1,000 bootstrapped proportions is roughly bell-shaped and centered at the observed $0.55,$ ranging from about $0.505$ to $0.602$; four of its percentiles are printed above.
    Using the distribution of 1,000 bootstrapped proportions, approximate a 92% confidence interval for the true proportion of shots at this level that are taken with the right foot, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.

3.  **Open-play shots, bootstrapping.** Emil Sørensen, briefing the network before the season, wants a defensible figure for how many chances arise from settled open play — as opposed to set pieces, throw-ins, counters, and the game's other patterns — since it shapes how much of a scout's attention should go to a prospect's set-piece behavior.
    At the 2022 Men's World Cup, 446 of the 1,494 shots — a proportion of $446/1494 = 0.299$ — arose from the `Regular Play` pattern.
    However, this value is based on a single tournament, so it may not be a perfect estimate for the population parameter of interest on its own.
    The seeded code below bootstraps the tournament's 1,494 shots 1,000 times.

    ```r
    wc2022_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv")

    wc2022_shots |>
      mutate(pattern = if_else(play_pattern == "Regular Play",
                               "regular play", "other")) |>
      count(pattern)
    #> # A tibble: 2 × 2
    #>   pattern          n
    #>   <chr>        <int>
    #> 1 other         1048
    #> 2 regular play   446

    set.seed(1207)
    openplay_boot <- wc2022_shots |>
      mutate(pattern = if_else(play_pattern == "Regular Play",
                               "regular play", "other")) |>
      specify(response = pattern, success = "regular play") |>
      generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
      calculate(stat = "prop")

    round(quantile(openplay_boot$stat, c(0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99)), 3)
    #>    1%    5%   95%   99%
    #> 0.270 0.279 0.318 0.327

    ggplot(openplay_boot, aes(x = stat)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
      labs(
        x = "Bootstrapped proportion of regular-play shots",
        y = "Count",
        title = "1,000 bootstrapped proportions"
      )
    ```

    The histogram of the 1,000 bootstrapped proportions is roughly bell-shaped and centered at the observed $0.299,$ ranging from about $0.262$ to $0.333$ — a narrow distribution, as we should expect with 1,494 observations behind each resample; four of its percentiles are printed above.
    Using the distribution of 1,000 bootstrapped proportions, approximate a 98% confidence interval for the true proportion of shots at this level that arise from regular open play, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.

4.  **Bootstrap distributions of** $\hat{p}$**, I.** Northbridge ran trial weeks at four partner academies, labelled A through D.
    Each cohort contained $n = 23$ trialists, and the coaching panel returned a "sign" or "pass" verdict on each — the seven-trialist bag of @sec-foundations-bootstrapping, scaled up.[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-3]
    The four cohorts' observed proportions of "sign" verdicts were, in no particular order:
    $$\hat{p} = 0.13 \ \ \hat{p} = 0.22 \ \ \hat{p} = 0.30 \ \ \hat{p} = 0.43.$$
    The seeded code below constructs the four cohorts — note that it *shuffles* which cohort receives which rate, so the assignment cannot be read off the construction; you must reason from the bootstrap summaries.
    It then bootstraps each cohort's sample 1,000 times and summarizes each of the four bootstrap distributions: `lower_95` and `upper_95` are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of its 1,000 $\hat{p}_{boot}$ values (the middle 95%), and `min` and `max` give its full range.
    Each distribution is unimodal and centered at its cohort's observed proportion, its values stepping in increments of $1/23$; the distribution nearest zero shows a mild right skew, since a proportion cannot fall below $0.$

    ```r
    set.seed(1247)
    p_hats <- sample(c(0.13, 0.22, 0.30, 0.43))  # shuffled to cohorts A-D

    make_cohort <- function(p) {
      n_sign <- round(23 * p)
      tibble(verdict = sample(c(rep("sign", n_sign),
                                rep("pass", 23 - n_sign))))
    }

    cohort_a <- make_cohort(p_hats[1])
    cohort_b <- make_cohort(p_hats[2])
    cohort_c <- make_cohort(p_hats[3])
    cohort_d <- make_cohort(p_hats[4])

    boot_cohort <- function(cohort) {
      set.seed(1208)
      cohort |>
        specify(response = verdict, success = "sign") |>
        generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
        calculate(stat = "prop")
    }

    bind_rows(
      A = boot_cohort(cohort_a),
      B = boot_cohort(cohort_b),
      C = boot_cohort(cohort_c),
      D = boot_cohort(cohort_d),
      .id = "cohort"
    ) |>
      group_by(cohort) |>
      summarize(
        lower_95 = quantile(stat, 0.025),
        upper_95 = quantile(stat, 0.975),
        min = min(stat),
        max = max(stat)
      )
    #> # A tibble: 4 × 5
    #>   cohort lower_95 upper_95   min   max
    #>   <chr>     <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
    #> 1 A        0         0.262 0     0.348
    #> 2 B        0.217     0.652 0.130 0.739
    #> 3 C        0.130     0.479 0     0.652
    #> 4 D        0.0870    0.391 0     0.478
    ```

    Treating the summary table as your only view of the four distributions — imagine you were handed the four histograms without the underlying counts — match each bootstrap distribution with the cohort's observed proportion of "sign" verdicts.

5.  **Bootstrap distributions of** $\hat{p}$**, II.** Consider again the four trial cohorts of the previous exercise, each with $n = 23$ verdicts, along with the summaries of their four bootstrap distributions (1,000 bootstrapped proportions each).
    Consider each of the following values for the true population proportion $p$ of "sign" verdicts among trialists of this kind.

6.  **Bootstrap distributions of** $\hat{p}$**, III.** Four of Emil's regional scouts — again labelled A through D — each tagged a sample of shots from the league they cover, recording whether each shot was a first-time effort.[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-4]
    Each scout found that exactly 40% of the shots in their sample were first-time efforts $(\hat{p} = 0.40),$ but the sample sizes differed: scout A tagged $n = 10$ shots, scout B $n = 100,$ scout C $n = 500,$ and scout D $n = 1000.$
    Each sample was bootstrapped 1,000 times with the seeded code below, which summarizes the four bootstrap distributions as in the previous exercises; each is roughly bell-shaped and centered at $0.40.$

    ```r
    tag_a <- tibble(shot = c(rep("first-time",   4), rep("other",   6)))
    tag_b <- tibble(shot = c(rep("first-time",  40), rep("other",  60)))
    tag_c <- tibble(shot = c(rep("first-time", 200), rep("other", 300)))
    tag_d <- tibble(shot = c(rep("first-time", 400), rep("other", 600)))

    boot_tags <- function(tagged) {
      set.seed(1209)
      tagged |>
        specify(response = shot, success = "first-time") |>
        generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") |>
        calculate(stat = "prop")
    }

    bind_rows(
      A = boot_tags(tag_a),
      B = boot_tags(tag_b),
      C = boot_tags(tag_c),
      D = boot_tags(tag_d),
      .id = "scout"
    ) |>
      group_by(scout) |>
      summarize(
        lower_95 = quantile(stat, 0.025),
        upper_95 = quantile(stat, 0.975),
        min = min(stat),
        max = max(stat)
      )
    #> # A tibble: 4 × 5
    #>   scout lower_95 upper_95   min   max
    #>   <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
    #> 1 A        0.1      0.7   0     0.9
    #> 2 B        0.3      0.5   0.27  0.58
    #> 3 C        0.354    0.438 0.332 0.474
    #> 4 D        0.37     0.431 0.354 0.449
    ```

    Consider each of the following values for the true population proportion $p$ of first-time shots in a league.
    For each parameter value, list the samples which could plausibly have come from a league with that proportion.
    (Hint: there may be more than one sample for each parameter value.)

    a.  $p = 0.05$

    b.  $p = 0.25$

    c.  $p = 0.45$

    d.  $p = 0.55$

    e.  $p = 0.75$

    Priya Rao audited a sample of recent requests and computed a 95% confidence interval for the mean generation time per prospect, from request to delivered pack, of (128 minutes, 147 minutes).[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-6]

S1. **Simulation workshop: does the interval keep its promise?** *A supplemental exercise, outside the IMS numbering: this time you build the simulation instead of reading one.*
Every "95% confident" in this chapter is a claim about the *procedure*: intervals built this way should capture the true parameter in about 95% of the samples we might have drawn.
For once that claim is checkable, by the census trick of this chapter's "watching the principle hold" box: the 2022 Men's World Cup is a fully logged population of 1,494 shots whose true conversion rate is known exactly, $p = 195/1494 = 0.1305.$
The seeded code below draws 500 samples of $n = 63$ shots — England's file size from the case study — builds a 95% percentile bootstrap interval from each sample (500 bootstrap resamples per interval), and records whether each interval captured $p.$

```r
wc2022_shots <- read_csv("data/derived/wc2022_shots.csv")
goals <- wc2022_shots$goal
p_true <- 195 / 1494

set.seed(1211)
captured <- replicate(500, {
  s <- sample(goals, 63)
  boot_p <- replicate(500, mean(sample(s, 63, replace = TRUE)))
  quantile(boot_p, 0.025) <= p_true & p_true <= quantile(boot_p, 0.975)
})

mean(captured)
#> [1] 0.918
```

a.  Before looking at the output: if the intervals kept their promise exactly, in about how many of the 500 samples should the interval capture the true conversion rate?

b.  The run above captures $p$ in 459 of the 500 samples, a capture rate of $0.918.$
    Is the shortfall an accident of this particular seed, or something systematic?
    Rerun the audit with two or three other seeds before you answer.

c.  Whatever you concluded in part (b), explain *why* a percentile interval built on 63 shots might fall short of its advertised coverage, and what a scout should do about the label when a file this small crosses their desk.
    (Hint: with 63 shots and a conversion rate near $0.13,$ a typical sample contains around 8 goals — count how many distinct values $\hat{p}_{boot}$ can then take. @sec-one-prop-null-boot will meet the same headcount problem from the mathematical side.)

[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-4]: The four tagged samples are a constructed scouting scenario, built entirely by the seeded code shown; the shot counts are not real league data.

[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-5]: The survey and its interval are a constructed scenario; no such league-wide survey exists.

[^_12-ex-foundations-bootstrapping-6]: The data-pack audit and its interval are a constructed scenario, used here as a premise for reasoning about a confidence interval for a mean.
